common_name: Wyant Plum (Historic Iowa Heirloom American Plum)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or grafted stock in late winter to early spring in full sun on well-drained soil, siting a second American plum cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Wyant emerged from the native-plum improvement movement that swept Iowa and the Upper Midwest in the 1870s-1880s, when nurserymen collected and named the best wild Prunus americana seedlings for home orchard use; it was documented alongside De Soto, Wolf, and Terry as one of the standout selections of that era in U.P. Hedrick's 1911 survey 'The Plums of New York.' The tree bears clusters of medium-to-large red fruit over firm yellow flesh with a tangy-sweet flavor well suited to jam and preserves, and like other heirloom native plums it is not reliably self-fruitful, so plant it with another American plum seedling or cultivar nearby. Expect vigorous root suckering that should be cut back to keep a single trunk, and expect the tree to tolerate Midwestern winters, drought, and poor soil far better than modern Japanese or European hybrid plums.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
U.P. Hedrick, The Plums of New York, New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, 1911
American Pomological Society historical fruit catalog records

common_name: Rollingstone Plum (Historic Minnesota Heirloom American Plum)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or grafted stock in early spring in full sun on well-drained soil; pair with another American plum for cross-pollination, since Rollingstone is self-incompatible.

directions: Named for the town of Rollingstone in southeastern Minnesota, this selection of wild Prunus americana was identified and propagated during the same late-19th-century wave of native-plum collecting that produced De Soto and Wyant, and it was prized specifically for surviving winters too harsh for most other named plums of its day. It bears small-to-medium dark red fruit over sweet-tart yellow flesh, used historically more for jelly and preserving than fresh eating, and it ripens reliably even in short, cool growing seasons. The tree suckers freely and tolerates thin, rocky prairie soils, making it a good choice for a hedgerow or windbreak planting as well as a home orchard where cold-hardiness matters more than fruit size.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension
U.P. Hedrick, The Plums of New York, New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, 1911
American Pomological Society historical fruit catalog records

common_name: Stoddard Plum (Historic Upper Midwest Heirloom American Plum)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or grafted stock in early spring in full sun on well-drained soil, siting a second American plum cultivar nearby for fruit set.

directions: Stoddard is one of the many named selections of wild Prunus americana that Upper Midwest nurserymen singled out during the 1870s-1880s native-plum boom, when settlers on the prairie needed cold-hardy fruit that could survive winters lethal to European and Japanese plums; it was recorded among the productive, widely planted varieties of that generation in Hedrick's 1911 'Plums of New York.' The tree produces medium red-skinned fruit over yellow flesh in heavy clusters and is valued chiefly for its reliability and productivity rather than dessert quality, making it a long-standing favorite for jam and canning in home orchards from Minnesota to the Dakotas. Remove root suckers periodically to maintain tree form, and pair with a second American plum cultivar since self-fruitfulness is poor.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension
U.P. Hedrick, The Plums of New York, New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, 1911
Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

common_name: Forest Garden Plum (Historic Iowa Heirloom American Plum)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or grafted stock in early spring in full sun on well-drained soil, with a second American plum nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Forest Garden was among the earliest widely distributed named selections of wild Prunus americana out of Iowa, part of the same 1870s native-plum improvement effort that later produced De Soto, Wyant, and Hawkeye, and it circulated through regional nursery catalogs for decades as a dependable prairie fruit tree. It bears medium red fruit with firm yellow flesh and good productivity, prized historically more for reliability in harsh climates than for refined flavor, and it was often planted as part of mixed fencerow or windbreak plantings as well as formal orchards. Like its sibling selections from the same era, it suckers readily and needs a cross-pollinator, but it shrugs off drought, cold, and neglect far better than most modern plum cultivars.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
U.P. Hedrick, The Plums of New York, New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, 1911
American Pomological Society historical fruit catalog records

common_name: Heath Cling Peach (Historic Southern White Clingstone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter before bud break in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Heath Cling needs a long, hot growing season to finish ripening properly.

directions: Heath Cling (often simply called Heath) dates to the early 1800s in Virginia and became one of the defining late-season clingstone peaches of the antebellum South, where it was treasured for its large, downy, creamy-white skin and rich, aromatic white flesh that holds together well under heat. Because it ripens very late in the season and demands a long run of warm days to develop full flavor, it is best suited to the mid-South and warmer mid-Atlantic rather than short-season Northern climates. Historically it was the preferred peach for home brandy-making and heavy syrup preserving, since the dense, non-browning flesh stands up to cooking far better than modern freestone peaches. Thin fruit after the June drop, prune to an open vase form for airflow in humid regions, and watch for brown rot as the long ripening window increases exposure.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Peach Cultivar History
North Carolina State University Extension — Heirloom Fruit Varieties
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange

common_name: Honey Peach (Historic Southern Flat Clingstone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter before bud break in well-drained soil in full sun; Honey has a low chill requirement and thrives in the warm, humid Deep South.

directions: Honey is a flattened, 'doughnut-shaped' white clingstone peach of Chinese origin that reached the American South in the mid-1800s through the same wave of introductions, centered on Augusta, Georgia nurseries, that brought in Chinese Cling, and it became a beloved dooryard heirloom for its intensely sweet, honeyed fragrance that perfumes a whole yard when the fruit ripens. The flattened fruit is small to medium with thin, often fuzzy-light skin and a flavor many growers describe as sweeter and more floral than any round-fruited peach of its era. It ripens quite early for a Southern heirloom and needs comparatively few chill hours, so it is best suited to the Deep South and Gulf Coast rather than colder regions. Thin fruit while small, since the flattened shape makes overcrowded clusters prone to splitting, and expect the tree itself to be more compact and spreading than a standard round-fruited peach.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Peach Cultivar History
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange
Monticello/Thomas Jefferson Foundation — Historic Fruit Varieties

common_name: Late Crawford Peach (Crawford's Late, Historic 19th-Century Freestone Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter before bud break in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Late Crawford needs roughly 700-750 chill hours and performs best in zones 5-8.

directions: Late Crawford was discovered in the early 1820s in the same New Jersey orchard that produced Early Crawford, and it went on to become one of the most important American peaches of the 19th century, grown commercially up and down the East Coast and used as breeding stock behind many later freestone cultivars. The fruit is large, deep yellow with a red blush, and freestone, ripening several weeks after its earlier sibling with a rich, sweet, old-fashioned peach flavor that many heirloom growers still rate above modern shipping cultivars. Because the fruit buds are only moderately cold-hardy and brown rot can be a problem in humid late-summer weather, thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart after the June drop, prune to an open vase form, and keep up a fungicide program through ripening.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Peach Cultivar History
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Prunus Germplasm Collection
Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Early Golden Apricot (Historic Northeastern Heirloom Apricot)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Early Golden is self-fertile but blooms very early and benefits from a sheltered site away from spring frost pockets.

directions: Early Golden is one of the oldest American-raised apricot cultivars, dating to the early-to-mid 1800s in New Jersey, and it was selected specifically because it could set and hold fruit in the humid, frost-prone Northeast where imported European apricots like Moorpark often failed. The tree produces small to medium golden-orange freestone fruit with sweet, mild flavor, and it is somewhat more tolerant of brown rot and humid summers than many larger-fruited European types, though its very early bloom still leaves it vulnerable to a late spring freeze in any given year. Site it in a protected spot with good air drainage to reduce frost risk, and expect self-fertility so no second tree is required for fruit set. It remains a favorite in Northeastern and Upper Midwest home orchards precisely because so few apricots tolerate that combination of cold winters and humid growing seasons.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Fruit Tree Varieties
Seed Savers Exchange

common_name: Alexander Apricot (Historic Russian-Type Hardy Heirloom Apricot)

planting.note: Plant bare-root in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Alexander blooms very early and is best sited where late frosts are less likely to catch the flowers.

directions: Alexander belongs to the group of cold-hardy Manchurian and Russian apricot types brought into the American Midwest in the 1870s-1880s as part of the broader effort to find fruit varieties tough enough for the Iowa and northern Plains winters, at a time when standard European apricots simply could not survive there. It is extremely cold-hardy for an apricot and blooms very early, which gives it a head start on the growing season but also exposes it to late-frost losses more often than later-blooming cultivars. The fruit is small, yellow-orange, and used mainly for preserves and drying rather than fresh market sale, with a flavor that is tangier and less refined than California-type apricots but entirely serviceable for home use. Because of the early bloom, growers in continental climates often plant it on a north-facing slope or near a windbreak to delay flowering by a few critical days.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Prunus Germplasm Collection
University of Minnesota Extension
